blocks.text: And Pliny uses it throughout, as in book 10, ch. 3, where he speaks of the haliaeetus: That which is born from them has its kind among the ossifrages. And a little later: Some add a kind of eagle which they call the bearded eagle; the Tuscans, however, call it the ossifrage. And again, where he speaks of the chicks [II, 773] that eagles throw out because they are weary of feeding them: When they have been thrown out by these, the related kind of the ossifrage takes them up and rears them with its own. And in ch. 7: Some think that the immussulus is the chick of the vulture, and the sanqualis that of the ossifrage. Likewise Massurius says that the sanqualis is the ossifrage. And in book 30, ch. 7: The ossifrage has a single intestine of wonderful nature, which digests everything it has swallowed. And a little before: The stomach of the ossifrage, dried and taken in drink, is very useful to those who do not digest their food. And in the chapter immediately following he prescribes that the same be taken to expel stones. Isidore too, book 12, ch. 7: The bird that drops bones from on high and breaks them is commonly called ossifrangus (read ossifragus), and hence it received its name from breaking bones. See also Festus under the words immussulus and sanqualis. Ossifragus is rendered in Greek in one Glossary as ὀστοκόπος [ostokopos], ὀστοκλάστης [ostoklastēs], ὀστοκατεάκτης [ostokateaktēs]; in another, but wrongly, as ὀστοκόραξ [ostokorax]; in Dioscorides as φίνις [phinis]. Φίνις [Phinis], he says, τὸ ὄρνεον, ὃ Ῥωμαϊστὶ καλοῦσιν ὀσσίφραγον [to orneon, ho Rhōmaisti kalousin ossiphragon]. And among older writers it is φήνη [phēnē], a word very well known from Homer and Aristotle, and one which the Arabs also use. Damir, from Ibnosaida: الفينة طاير يشبه العقاب فاذا خاف البرد انحدر الي اليمن [al-fīna ṭāyir yushbih al-ʿuqāb fa-idhā khāfa al-bard inḥadara ilā al-Yaman] Phena, a bird resembling the eagle, which, when it fears the cold, goes off to Ieman, that is, to Arabia Felix. But it is commonly called, as we have said, كاسر [kāsir] breaker, and كاسر اعظام [kāsir aʿẓām] breaker of bones. Also مكلفة [mukallafa] mechalapha, from its black colour mixed with reddish or yellowish. Damir: الكاسر العقاب [al-kāsir al-ʿuqāb] Alchasir (or breaker) is a kind of eagle. The same elsewhere: كاسر العظام المكلفة [kāsir al-ʿiẓām al-mukallafa] The breaker of bones, that is, the mechalepha. And in the chapter On the mechalepha: الفرخ الذي ترمي [col. 188] به العقاب من الثلثة يحضنه طاير يقال له المكلفه ويقال له كاسر العظام وتربيه [al-farkh alladhī tarmī bihi al-ʿuqāb min al-thalatha yaḥḍunuhu ṭāyir yuqāl lahu al-mukallafa wa-yuqāl lahu kāsir al-ʿiẓām wa-turabbīhi] The chick which the eagle has thrown out of the three is warmed and fed by a bird which is called mechalepha and breaker of bones. And in the chapter العقاب [al-ʿuqāb], or On the eagle: والعرب يسمي العقاب الكاسر [wa-al-ʿarab yusammī al-ʿuqāb al-kāsir] The Arabs also call the eagle (that is, a species of eagle) the breaker. And below: والفرخ الذي تلقيه يعطف عليه طاير يسمي كاسر العظام ويسمي المكلفه ايضا فيربيه [wa-al-farkh alladhī tulqīhi yaʿṭifu ʿalayhi ṭāyir yusammā kāsir al-ʿiẓām wa-yusammā al-mukallafa ayḍan fa-yurabbīhi] And on the chick thrown out by the eagle a bird takes pity, which is named ossifrage and mechalepha, so that it rears it. It is evident that the French orfraye is derived from ossifraga, although among us it denotes something else, namely the haliaeetus or sea eagle. This was observed long ago by Belon, On Birds, book 2, ch. 7.
